2026-09-13, E2-T72: BUILT on Circle.FromBestFit's fit, with only the sweep new. FITTING IS A QUESTION ABOUT A CIRCLE AND THE SWEEP IS A QUESTION ABOUT ORDER, so the two are answered separately and the fit cannot be affected by the ordering. The sweep is accumulated step by step, each step the short way round, so points that cross the plane's x axis trace the arc they were sampled from - a first-to-last angle difference reads 350 to 20 degrees as minus 330 instead of plus 30. POINTS THAT DOUBLE BACK ARE REFUSED rather than fitted to whatever their shuffled angles sum to: shuffled points still have a perfectly good circle through them, so the fit succeeds and only the sweep is nonsense, which is exactly the shape of failure that gets shipped.

2026-09-13, E2-T41 step B: composed - Plane.FromOriginNormal turns the centre and the normal into the plane the factory takes. SPARK MAKES THE ANGLE DATUM EXPLICIT and Dynamo leaves it implicit: a centre and a normal do not say where angle zero is, and a plane does.

2026-09-14, E2-T72: BUILT, reducing to FromCenterStartPointSweepAngle as the row said it would. THE DECISION THE ROW DID NOT MAKE IS THE OVER-DETERMINATION, and it is now made and written into the remarks: a centre, a start and an end do NOT generally lie on a common circle, because the end is at a different distance from the centre than the start. The radius comes from the START and the end point is used only for the DIRECTION it lies in, so the arc finishes on the ray towards it. A caller handing in three measured points gets an arc that misses the third, and the remarks say why. The sweep is the shorter way round, which is stated rather than implied; the explicit-angle factory is there for the major arc. THE BRANCH IS THAT OVER-DETERMINATION: the test whose end point sits at radius 7 while the start is at radius 2 pins it, and a mutation that uses the end point directly turns six tests red because the result is not an arc about that centre at all. Exposed as the node Arc.FromCenterStartEnd.
2026-09-13, E2-T41 step B: argument for argument, with the normal carried as a Vector3d and the sweep as an Angle (ADR-0011).

2026-09-13, E2-T72: BUILT, and it is the GENERAL two-curve fillet the row asked for rather than the two-line one. FilletLines stopped where it did for a reason it stated in its own remarks - a general fillet needs curve-curve intersection to find the corner, and an iterative tangency solve, NEITHER OF WHICH EXISTED THEN. E2-T11 built the first and this step wrote the second, so the stated stopping point expired. THE METHOD: the fillet centre is the point at distance r from BOTH curves, which is where their offsets cross - CurveOffset.Offset plus Curve.IntersectWith, both of which exist. Four side combinations give four such points and the nearest to the corner is the fillet the caller meant; the other three round off its reflections. That intersection is a SEED and not the answer, because Offset is exact only for Line, Circle and Arc and fits a curve for everything else: the centre is refined by Newton on distance(c, first) = r and distance(c, second) = r, whose gradients are the unit vectors from the closest points, so the step is a 2x2 solve. Without it a fillet is tangent only to the fit's accuracy, and tangency is the whole of what a fillet promises. Spark asks for the PLANE NORMAL where Dynamo infers it, because two straight curves have no plane of their own - Curve.PlaneOf returns null for a line, which is E2-T71 family (2)'s answer arriving here.

2026-09-14, E2-T72: BUILT, and the row's own prediction held exactly - THE SAME SOLVE WITH ONE MORE ROW. CurveOffset.Fillet is GIVEN the radius and solves for a centre at that distance from two curves: two equations, two unknowns. This is not given it, so the unknowns are the centre's two in-plane coordinates AND the radius, and the equations are distance(c, curve_i) = r for all three. The gradient of a distance-to-curve is the unit vector from the closest point, so each Jacobian row is that vector's two components followed by -1 - the SAME column in every row, because moving the radius moves all three residuals together, which is what makes the system solvable rather than over-determined. A 3x3 Cramer solve, chosen over elimination because at three the determinant is the clearest way to say 'singular', and a zero one means two curves are tangent to each other at the centre and bound no corner. THREE CURVES HAVE SEVERAL CIRCLES TANGENT TO ALL OF THEM - a triangle has four - SO THE SEED DECIDES WHICH COMES BACK, and it is stated rather than left to the solver: the CENTROID OF THE THREE PAIRWISE CROSSINGS, radius seeded as the mean distance from there to the three curves. For a triangle that point is inside it, so the INCIRCLE is the answer and the three excircles are not. Replacing the seed with an endpoint of the first curve reddens six of the eight tests. NOTHING IS TRIMMED, unlike Fillet: that member rounds a corner and hands back the two curves cut to meet the arc, while this one answers a question about SIZE and returns the arc alone. The third curve contributes no endpoint, so the arc still runs between its tangent points on the first two - which the tests assert, because swapping which curve is the constraint gives the SAME circle and a different quarter of it. THE ANCHOR IS A 3-4-5 TRIANGLE, whose incircle radius is area over semiperimeter, 6/6 = 1 EXACTLY, centred at (1, 1) with the right angle at the origin - derived by hand rather than read off the implementation, and an equilateral triangle of side 6 gives side/(2*sqrt 3) beside it. A mutation that ignores the third curve cannot produce either and reddens five. A CURVED constraint has its own test, so the member is not pinned to straight lines. Exposed as the node Curve.FilletTangentTo.

2026-09-13, E2-T41 step B: AN ARC HAS THREE DEGREES OF FREEDOM IN ITS PLANE AND THIS GIVES FOUR CONSTRAINTS, so either the second tangent is advisory, or the result is a biarc rather than an arc, or the call fails when they disagree. Which one is not deducible from a signature, and the manifest is metadata. Recorded in §6.3.

2026-09-14, E2-T72: BUILT, and UNLIKE THE CENTRE FORM IT IS WELL POSED - two points and a direction determine exactly one arc, so this one passes through BOTH points exactly. The centre is where the chord's perpendicular bisector meets the line through the start perpendicular to the tangent, which reduces to a single division rather than a solve. A TANGENT ALONG THE CHORD IS REFUSED rather than straightened: the two perpendiculars are parallel, there is no centre, and the shape wanted is a straight line - returning an arc of enormous radius pretending to be one would be the worse answer. Both directions along the chord are refused and both are tested. THE BRANCH IS THE TANGENT: an implementation that merely joined the two points satisfies every assertion about position, so the test asserts the direction the arc leaves the start in to 1e-9, and the mutation that ignores the tangent turns that test red. A perpendicular tangent gives the semicircle, which is the case with an answer known by hand. Exposed as the node Arc.FromStartEndStartTangent.

2026-09-13, E2-T72: BUILT, as TWO fits in two stages - the points are almost never coplanar, so Plane.FromBestFit first and the circle within it. THE CIRCLE FIT IS ALGEBRAIC THEN REFINED GEOMETRICALLY, AND THE SECOND HALF IS NOT DECORATION: the algebraic (Kasa) fit is a 3x3 solve and is EXACT for points that lie on a circle, but under noise on a SHORT ARC it systematically under-estimates the radius, because squaring the distance weights the far points hardest and a short arc has no far side to balance them. Measured rather than cited: removing the Gauss-Newton refinement makes a 20-degree arc of radius 10 with a 0.5% wobble fit a mean radius of 9.58. The refinement minimises the distance residual anybody fitting a circle actually means, converges in a handful of steps from that seed, and moves nothing when the seed is already exact.
